category: Nouns that come in gender pairs

entries.meaning: Someone who performs in plays or films.
examples: She is one of the finest actors of her generation.
Both actors trained at the same school.
The actors were still rehearsing at midnight.
She won Best Actress that year.
Many actresses now ask to be called actors.

senses.head: A performer of any sex
examples: She is one of the finest actors of her generation.
Both actors trained at the same school.
The actors were still rehearsing at midnight.

senses.head: The marked feminine form
examples: She won Best Actress that year.
Many actresses now ask to be called actors.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the actors were rehearsing
entries.variants: actress /ˈæktrɪs/ is still used, especially in award categories
entries.contrast: Actor now covers performers of any sex, and most performers prefer it. Actress survives mainly because award shows keep separate categories. Neither is wrong, but actor is the safe default.

entries.meaning: Someone who serves food in a restaurant.
examples: Ask the waiter for the check.
Both waiters were run off their feet.
The servers here work for tips. (neutral)
Our waitress recommended the special.
Two waitresses covered the whole patio.

senses.head: The neutral or male form
examples: Ask the waiter for the check.
Both waiters were run off their feet.
The servers here work for tips. (neutral)

senses.head: The marked feminine form
examples: Our waitress recommended the special.
Two waitresses covered the whole patio.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the waiters were overwhelmed
entries.variants: waitress /ˈweɪtrɪs/ is still common; server is the neutral American term
entries.contrast: In American restaurants server has largely replaced both. Waitress is not offensive and is still widely used, but server is what most restaurants say now.

entries.meaning: Someone who receives guests, or presents a program.
examples: Our host met us at the door.
Both hosts of the show were replaced.
The hosts had prepared far too much food.
The hostess showed us to a table.
Two hostesses worked the front of house.

senses.head: The neutral form
examples: Our host met us at the door.
Both hosts of the show were replaced.
The hosts had prepared far too much food.

senses.head: The marked feminine form
examples: The hostess showed us to a table.
Two hostesses worked the front of house.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the hosts greeted everyone
entries.variants: hostess /ˈhoʊstɪs/ survives in restaurants and on airlines
entries.contrast: Host is neutral and covers everyone. Hostess is still used for the person who seats guests in a restaurant, and in air hostess, which is itself being replaced by flight attendant.

entries.meaning: Someone who looks after passengers; also a manager of property.
examples: The flight attendants prepared the cabin. (current term)
Airlines stopped saying stewardess decades ago.
My grandmother was a stewardess in the 1960s.
He is a careful steward of the endowment.
Union stewards handle member complaints.

senses.head: The aviation sense
examples: The flight attendants prepared the cabin. (current term)
Airlines stopped saying stewardess decades ago.
My grandmother was a stewardess in the 1960s.

senses.head: A manager or caretaker
examples: He is a careful steward of the endowment.
Union stewards handle member complaints.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the stewards were trained in first aid
entries.variants: stewardess /ˈstuːərdɪs/ is now dated; flight attendant has replaced both
entries.contrast: This pair has been almost completely replaced in aviation by flight attendant, which is the term airlines and staff use. Stewardess now sounds distinctly mid-century.

entries.meaning: A woman whose spouse has died.
examples: She was left a widow at thirty-four.
Both widows received the same pension.
War widows were granted special status.
He has been a widower for six years.
Two widowers in the building married each other's neighbors.

senses.head: The bereaved woman
examples: She was left a widow at thirty-four.
Both widows received the same pension.
War widows were granted special status.

senses.head: The male counterpart
examples: He has been a widower for six years.
Two widowers in the building married each other's neighbors.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the widows received pensions
entries.variants: the male counterpart is widower /ˈwɪdoʊər/
entries.contrast: This pair is fully alive and unmarked in either direction. Unusually, the male form is the derived one: widower is built from widow, not the other way around.

entries.meaning: A woman on her wedding day.
examples: The bride arrived twenty minutes late.
Both brides wore their mothers' dresses.
The brides posed together for a photograph.
The groom forgot the rings.
Both bridegrooms gave short speeches.

senses.head: The woman marrying
examples: The bride arrived twenty minutes late.
Both brides wore their mothers' dresses.
The brides posed together for a photograph.

senses.head: The male counterpart
examples: The groom forgot the rings.
Both bridegrooms gave short speeches.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the brides posed together
entries.variants: the male counterpart is groom or bridegroom
entries.contrast: Fully alive. Note that groom is a shortening of bridegroom, which is itself built on bride — the same asymmetry as widow/widower. Groom also separately means someone who cares for horses.

entries.meaning: A married man, considered in relation to his spouse.
examples: Her husband teaches at the college.
Both husbands stayed home with the children.
He has been a good husband to her.
Each employee may add one spouse to the plan.
Both partners signed the lease.

senses.head: The married man
examples: Her husband teaches at the college.
Both husbands stayed home with the children.
He has been a good husband to her.

senses.head: The neutral cover term
examples: Each employee may add one spouse to the plan.
Both partners signed the lease.

entries.agreement: plural verb — their husbands stayed home
entries.variants: the female counterpart is wife, plural wives — see wife
entries.contrast: Fully alive, and the neutral cover term is spouse or partner, which many couples now prefer. Note the irregular plural on the other half of the pair: wife → wives.

entries.meaning: A male monarch.
examples: The king abdicated in 1936.
Both kings claimed the same territory.
Three kings ruled in a single decade.
The queen reigned for seventy years.
Two queens ruled in their own right.

senses.head: The monarch
examples: The king abdicated in 1936.
Both kings claimed the same territory.
Three kings ruled in a single decade.

senses.head: The female counterpart
examples: The queen reigned for seventy years.
Two queens ruled in their own right.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the kings met at the border
entries.variants: the female counterpart is queen
entries.contrast: Fully alive. Note the asymmetry in meaning: a queen may be a ruler in her own right or a king's wife, while a king is always a ruler. The wife of a reigning queen is a prince consort, not a king.

entries.meaning: The son of a monarch, or a ruler of a small state.
examples: The prince was educated abroad.
Both princes renounced their claims.
Three princes attended the funeral.
The princess opened the new hospital.
Both princesses married commoners.

senses.head: The male title
examples: The prince was educated abroad.
Both princes renounced their claims.
Three princes attended the funeral.

senses.head: The female counterpart
examples: The princess opened the new hospital.
Both princesses married commoners.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the princes were educated abroad
entries.variants: the female counterpart is princess /ˈprɪnsɛs/
entries.contrast: A live pair, since it names a hereditary title where sex is part of the definition. Unlike actress, princess is not going anywhere.

entries.meaning: A nobleman of the highest rank below a monarch.
examples: The duke held estates in three counties.
Both dukes sat in the House of Lords.
Several dukes were created that year.
The duchess opened the gardens to visitors.
Two duchesses attended the ceremony.

senses.head: The male title
examples: The duke held estates in three counties.
Both dukes sat in the House of Lords.
Several dukes were created that year.

senses.head: The female counterpart
examples: The duchess opened the gardens to visitors.
Two duchesses attended the ceremony.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the dukes held vast estates
entries.variants: the female counterpart is duchess /ˈdʌtʃɪs/
entries.contrast: Note that the feminine form changes the stem, not just the ending: duke → duchess, not ✗ dukess. A duchess may hold the title herself or be a duke's wife.

entries.meaning: The ruler of an empire.
examples: The emperor ruled for forty-one years.
Both emperors were deified after death.
Several emperors reigned within a single year.
The empress governed in his absence.
Two empresses ruled in their own right.

senses.head: The male title
examples: The emperor ruled for forty-one years.
Both emperors were deified after death.
Several emperors reigned within a single year.

senses.head: The female counterpart
examples: The empress governed in his absence.
Two empresses ruled in their own right.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the emperors were deified
entries.variants: the female counterpart is empress /ˈɛmprɪs/
entries.contrast: Like duke/duchess, the feminine form contracts the stem: emperor → empress, not ✗ emperoress.

entries.meaning: Someone admired for courage; the main character of a story.
examples: The firefighters were treated as heroes.
She's a hero to everyone in that department.
Both heroes refused any recognition.
The novel's heroine narrates the whole story.
Both heroines end up disillusioned.

senses.head: The neutral form
examples: The firefighters were treated as heroes.
She's a hero to everyone in that department.
Both heroes refused any recognition.

senses.head: The literary feminine form
examples: The novel's heroine narrates the whole story.
Both heroines end up disillusioned.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the heroes were honored
entries.variants: the female counterpart is heroine /ˈhɛroʊɪn/
entries.contrast: Hero now covers everyone, and a brave woman is normally called a hero. Heroine survives mainly in literary criticism, meaning the main female character. Note the pronunciation trap: heroine /ˈhɛroʊɪn/ is spelled almost identically to heroin, the drug, and they sound the same.

entries.meaning: The person who leads a meeting or organization.
examples: The chairman called the meeting to order.
Both chairmen resigned the same week.
She has been chair of the department since 2020.
Both chairpersons signed the report.
The chairwoman set a three-minute limit on questions.

senses.head: The traditional male form
examples: The chairman called the meeting to order.
Both chairmen resigned the same week.

senses.head: The neutral forms
examples: She has been chair of the department since 2020.
Both chairpersons signed the report.
The chairwoman set a three-minute limit on questions.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the chairmen met privately
entries.variants: neutral forms are chair, chairperson, and for a woman chairwoman
entries.contrast: In American professional usage chair is now the default: she chairs the committee, the chair recognized the senator. Chairman is still correct but reads as traditional or male-specific. Note the plural takes the mutation plural of man: chairmen, not ✗ chairmans.

entries.meaning: Someone who speaks on behalf of an organization.
examples: A company spokesman denied the report.
Both spokesmen gave identical statements.
A spokesperson confirmed the layoffs.
The spokeswoman refused to take questions.
Both spokespersons were quoted anonymously.

senses.head: The traditional male form
examples: A company spokesman denied the report.
Both spokesmen gave identical statements.

senses.head: The neutral and feminine forms
examples: A spokesperson confirmed the layoffs.
The spokeswoman refused to take questions.
Both spokespersons were quoted anonymously.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the spokesmen gave identical statements
entries.variants: neutral form spokesperson; feminine spokeswoman
entries.contrast: Spokesperson is now standard in American journalism, and news organizations use it by default unless the person's sex is relevant and known.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is selling.
examples: A car salesman called three times.
Both salesmen worked entirely on commission.
Every salesperson met quota this quarter.
The saleswoman knew the product cold.
Two sales reps cover the whole territory.

senses.head: The traditional male form
examples: A car salesman called three times.
Both salesmen worked entirely on commission.

senses.head: The neutral and feminine forms
examples: Every salesperson met quota this quarter.
The saleswoman knew the product cold.
Two sales reps cover the whole territory.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the salesmen worked on commission
entries.variants: neutral forms salesperson, sales representative, sales rep; feminine saleswoman
entries.contrast: Salesperson and sales rep are the normal terms in American business now. Salesman survives in the title of the play Death of a Salesman and in casual speech.

entries.meaning: A member of a police force.
examples: A policeman took the statement.
Both policemen were first on the scene.
Two police officers responded to the call.
The policewoman who arrested him testified.
Every police officer wears a body camera now.

senses.head: The traditional male form
examples: A policeman took the statement.
Both policemen were first on the scene.

senses.head: The neutral and feminine forms
examples: Two police officers responded to the call.
The policewoman who arrested him testified.
Every police officer wears a body camera now.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the policemen were first on the scene
entries.variants: neutral form police officer; feminine policewoman
entries.contrast: Police officer is the standard American term and what departments themselves use. Note also that police as a collective is always plural: the police are investigating.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is putting out fires.
examples: Firefighters worked through the night.
Both firefighters were treated for smoke inhalation.
She has been a firefighter for eleven years.
Two firemen carried the ladder between them.
Most departments stopped saying fireman long ago.

senses.head: The neutral form
examples: Firefighters worked through the night.
Both firefighters were treated for smoke inhalation.
She has been a firefighter for eleven years.

senses.head: The older form
examples: Two firemen carried the ladder between them.
Most departments stopped saying fireman long ago.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the firefighters worked through the night
entries.variants: the older term is fireman, plural firemen
entries.contrast: This replacement is essentially complete in American English: departments, news reports, and firefighters themselves say firefighter. Fireman now sounds like a children's book. Note that the replacement is a regular noun, so it escapes the -man → -men mutation plural.

entries.meaning: A woman in a religious order.
examples: The nuns ran the school for eighty years.
Both nuns took vows the same year.
She became a nun at twenty-three.
The monks keep silence until noon.
Two monks tend the entire garden.

senses.head: The religious woman
examples: The nuns ran the school for eighty years.
Both nuns took vows the same year.
She became a nun at twenty-three.

senses.head: The male counterpart
examples: The monks keep silence until noon.
Two monks tend the entire garden.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the nuns ran the school
entries.variants: the male counterpart is monk, not ✗ nunner
entries.contrast: A suppletive pair — the two words are unrelated in form, like king/queen and boy/girl. There is no shared stem.

entries.meaning: The daughter of one's sibling.
examples: His nieces visit every summer.
Both nieces were named after their grandmother.
She left everything to her niece.
Two nephews inherited the farm.
Her nephew is starting college.

senses.head: The relative
examples: His nieces visit every summer.
Both nieces were named after their grandmother.
She left everything to her niece.

senses.head: The male counterpart
examples: Two nephews inherited the farm.
Her nephew is starting college.

entries.agreement: plural verb — his nieces visit every summer
entries.variants: the male counterpart is nephew /ˈnɛfjuː/
entries.contrast: Another suppletive pair with no shared stem. Note the spelling follows the i-before-e rule, and the pronunciation is /niːs/, a homophone of Nice the French city.

entries.meaning: A man engaged to be married.
examples: Her fiancé proposed in October.
Both fiancés were introduced that evening.
She brought her fiancé to the reunion.
His fiancée is finishing law school.
Both fiancées chose the same venue.

senses.head: The engaged man
examples: Her fiancé proposed in October.
Both fiancés were introduced that evening.
She brought her fiancé to the reunion.

senses.head: The female counterpart
examples: His fiancée is finishing law school.
Both fiancées chose the same venue.

entries.agreement: plural verb — their fiancés met at the party
entries.variants: the female counterpart is fiancée, spelled with two e's
entries.contrast: The rare English pair distinguished only in spelling — fiancé and fiancée are pronounced identically. One e for a man, two for a woman, following French. Many American writers drop the accents entirely.
